Belgium.summary: The region lay in the Frankish lands: Austrasia, the eastern Frankish kingdom, covered present-day Belgium among other areas, while Neustria lay to the west. The Merovingian kingdoms fought one another until Chlothar II, king of Neustria, became sole ruler of the Franks in 613, and his son Dagobert I ruled the whole realm from 629.

events.t: Chilperic I is assassinated; his infant son Chlothar II succeeds, protected by his mother Fredegund.
Chlothar II becomes sole ruler of the Franks.
Dagobert I becomes king of all the Franks.

Denmark.polity: Magnates and chieftains (Late Germanic Iron Age)
Denmark.summary: This is the Late Germanic Iron Age (c. 550–800). Magnates ran power centres that controlled religion, trade and crafts. Gudme on Funen, with a magnate's farm, nearly 50 smaller farms, gold hoards and a coastal trading place at Lundeborg, flourished from the 3rd to the 7th century. A rich Nordic animal-art style developed, and the first images of the Nordic gods appear.

events.t: Gudme on Funen, a magnate's seat and cult centre with its trading place at Lundeborg, is in its final phase (3rd–7th centuries).

Finland.polity: Permanently settled communities in the south and west; hunter-fishers in the north (no state)
Finland.summary: Archaeologists call this the Merovingian period (c. 550–800). Permanent settlement was concentrated in southern and western Finland, including Ostrobothnia, while the far north had no permanent settlement and was used by hunting and fishing groups, called Lapps (Sámi) in older scholarship. In Ostrobothnia, finds are poorer than in the preceding Migration Period and western contacts declined. Evidence is almost entirely archaeological.

events.t: Ostrobothnian finds become fewer and poorer than in the Migration Period, reflecting weaker contacts with central Sweden.

sources.title: Liisa Erä-Esko, "On the Iron Age Settlement of Northern Finland", Iskos

France.summary: Gaul was ruled by Merovingian kings whose kingdoms often fought one another; Guntram of Burgundy tried to keep a balance among his warring relatives. Chlothar II, king of Neustria, became sole ruler of the Franks in 613, and his son Dagobert I ruled the whole realm from 629. Bishop Gregory of Tours wrote his Ten Books of history, and the Irish monk Columbanus founded Annegray and Luxeuil in the Vosges.

events.t: Columbanus, newly arrived from Ireland, founds Annegray in the Vosges, then Luxeuil and Fontaine.
Gregory of Tours, bishop and historian, dies (594?).
Chlothar II becomes sole ruler of the Franks.
Dagobert I becomes king of all the Franks.

Germany.polity: Merovingian Franks (Austrasia), with Alemanni, Thuringians and Bavarians; independent pagan Saxons
Germany.summary: The Rhineland and parts of western and central Germany belonged to Austrasia, the eastern Frankish kingdom. Other Germanic peoples lived farther east: Saxons between the Rhine and Elbe, Thuringians in central Germany and Alemanni on the upper Rhine, while the Bavarians were under Frankish influence. The Saxons clung to their pagan religion. Dagobert I became king of Austrasia in 623 and campaigned against the Slavs on his eastern frontier.

events.t: Theuderic II of Burgundy, backed by Brunhild, overthrows his brother Theudebert II of Austrasia.
Dagobert I becomes king of Austrasia.
Dagobert I's army is defeated by the Slavs under Samo at Wogastisburg (date as given by Fredegar).

Iceland.summary: Iceland had no settled human population in these decades. Britannica notes that Iceland apparently has no prehistory: the oldest written source, Íslendingabók (c. 1130), places Norse settlement in about 870–930, some two and a half centuries after this period.

events.t: Iceland remains uninhabited; Norse settlement begins only around 870.

Ireland.summary: Ireland had been Christian since the 5th century, and its monasteries were centres of classical learning that Irish monks carried abroad. Columba, who founded a monastery on Iona about 563, died there in 597; his elegy is probably by the chief poet Dallán Forgaill. Columbanus, trained at Bangor, left Ireland with twelve companions in 591 and founded monasteries in Gaul and at Bobbio in Italy.

events.t: Columbanus leaves Ireland for the Continent with twelve companions.
Columba dies on Iona.

Italy.polity: Lombard kingdom and duchies; Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna; papal Rome
Italy.summary: Italy was divided after the Lombards invaded in 568. They soon held most of the peninsula, but many small dukedoms grew up, while Rome, Ravenna and a few other fortified cities resisted and stayed with Byzantium. Pope Gregory I (590–604) defended Rome against the Lombards and sent Augustine to England. The Irish monk Columbanus went to the Lombard king Agilulf and founded the monastery of Bobbio.

events.t: The Lombards under Alboin invade Italy from Pannonia.
Gregory I is unanimously chosen pope.
Gregory I defends Rome against the Lombards (590s).
Columbanus founds the monastery of Bobbio (613 or 614).

Luxembourg.summary: The region lay in Austrasia, the eastern Frankish kingdom, ruled from 561 to 613 by Sigebert I and his descendants. Austrasia was caught up in Merovingian civil wars: in 612 Theuderic II of Burgundy, backed by Brunhild, overthrew Theudebert II of Austrasia, and in 613 Chlothar II became sole ruler of the Franks. In 623 Dagobert I was made king of Austrasia.

events.t: Theuderic II of Burgundy overthrows his brother Theudebert II of Austrasia.
Chlothar II becomes sole ruler of the Franks, including Austrasia.
Dagobert I becomes king of Austrasia.

Netherlands.polity: Frisians on the coast; Franks to the south
Netherlands.summary: The Frisians, a Germanic seafaring people, held the coastlands from the Rhine to the Ems. The Franks, centred on the lower Rhine, conquered them only gradually, completing the conquest in the 9th century, so in this period the Frisian coast lay outside Frankish rule.

events.t: Frisians, not yet under Frankish rule, hold the coast between the Rhine and the Ems.

Norway.polity: Local elites, no known central authority (Merovingian period, c. 550–800)
Norway.summary: Norwegian archaeologists call c. 550–800 the Merovingian period, a time of marked change in burial rites, language, art style and weaponry. Relatively few finds survive from it. Large burial mounds served as symbols of power and wealth, and the first Scandinavian ship burials appear early in the period. There is no contemporary written history, so knowledge is archaeological.

events.t: Burial rites, art style and weaponry change markedly as the Merovingian period (c. 550–800) unfolds.

sources.title: Scandinavia's oldest known ship burial is located in mid-Norway

Portugal.polity: Suebic kingdom in the northwest, absorbed by the Visigoths in 585
Portugal.summary: In the northwest the Suebi had an independent kingdom in Galicia. Once Arian, they were converted to Catholic Christianity in the mid-6th century by Martin of Dumio, bishop of Braga. In 585 the Visigoths under Leovigild conquered the kingdom, and the region became part of Visigothic Spain; the Visigoths already held part of Lusitania to the south.

events.t: The Visigothic king Leovigild conquers the Suebic kingdom.
The Visigothic kingdom, now including the former Suebic lands, formally converts from Arian to Catholic Christianity.

Spain.polity: Visigothic kingdom of Toledo (with Byzantine territory in the southeast until the 620s)
Spain.summary: The Visigoths ruled from Toledo. Leovigild (568–586) conquered the Suebi, and his son Reccared (586–601) abandoned Arianism for Catholicism, removing a main obstacle between Goths and Hispano-Romans. Isidore, bishop of Seville from about 600 to 636, wrote the encyclopaedic Etymologies. Between about 612 and 616 King Sisebut decreed that all Jews must convert, and Swinthila (621–631) took the last Byzantine fortresses.

events.t: Leovigild conquers the Suebic kingdom in the northwest.
The Visigoths formally convert from Arian to Catholic Christianity under Reccared.
Isidore becomes bishop of Seville (c. 600); he later writes the Etymologies.
Between about 612 and 616 King Sisebut decrees that all Jews of the kingdom must convert to Christianity.
Swinthila (621–631) conquers the last Byzantine fortresses in Spain (exact date uncertain).

sources.title: Spain (Chapter 5), The Jews in Late Antiquity

Sweden.summary: This is the Vendel period, named after the boat-grave cemetery at Vendel in Uppland; nearby Valsgärde held unlooted boat graves with rare helmets. The Svear lived around Lake Mälaren and Uppsala, the Götar in Östergötland and Västergötland. At Gamla Uppsala, great mounds and a magnate estate with a hall arose from the late 6th century. Gotland raised carved picture stones. There is no contemporary written history.

events.t: Vendel-period boat graves at Valsgärde, near Gamla Uppsala, contain helmets and rich weapons of a warrior elite.
Gamla Uppsala's East and West mounds are built in the late 6th–early 7th century as the site becomes a monumental centre.
Gotlanders carve picture stones in Vendel-period style; the early tradition is dated from the 5th to mid-7th century.

sources.title: John Ljungkvist & Per Frölund, "Gamla Uppsala – the emergence of a centre and a magnate complex", Journal of Archaeology and Ancient History 16 (2015)
Frederic B. Pearl, "The Water Dragon and the Snake Witch: Two Vendel Period Picture Stones from Gotland, Sweden", Current Swedish Archaeology

Switzerland.polity: Frankish kingdom of Burgundy (west) and Alamannic lands (north and east)
Switzerland.summary: The west belonged to the Frankish kingdom of Burgundy. Marius, bishop of Avenches from 573, wrote a world chronicle for 455–581 and is credited, without firm proof, with moving the see to Lausanne. To the north and east lay Alamannic lands, where Columbanus and his companions preached around 610–612. His companion Gall stayed behind and built a hermit's cell on the Steinach, the origin of the abbey of Saint Gall.

events.t: Marius, bishop of Avenches and author of a chronicle, dies.
Gall, a companion of Columbanus, stays behind and builds a hermit's cell on the Steinach near Arbon.
Chlothar II becomes sole ruler of the Franks, including Burgundy.

sources.title: Gall (saint)
sources.publisher: Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz (Dictionnaire historique de la Suisse)

United Kingdom.polity: Anglo-Saxon kingdoms (Kent, East Anglia, Northumbria and others); Christian Britons in Wales; Iona in the west
United Kingdom.summary: England was divided among Anglo-Saxon kingdoms, while Christian churches in Wales predated the Roman mission and Columba's monastery of Iona worked to convert Scotland. Pope Gregory I sent Augustine to Kent in 597, where King Æthelberht received him and was soon baptized. Æthelfrith, king of Bernicia from 592/593, also ruled Deira, together forming Northumbria. The Sutton Hoo ship burial (early 7th century) may be that of Rædwald of East Anglia.

events.t: Augustine's mission, sent by Pope Gregory I, reaches Kent and is received by King Æthelberht.
Æthelfrith, king of Bernicia and Deira (Northumbria), dies (date uncertain).
The Sutton Hoo ship burial is made (coins point to c. 610–635); Rædwald is a popular but unproven candidate.

sources.title: The Anglo-Saxon ship burial at Sutton Hoo

Greenland.polity: Uninhabited (gap between Early and Late Dorset)
Greenland.summary: Greenland appears to have been empty of people in these decades. Early Dorset Palaeo-Inuit had lived there until around the start of the common era, then abandoned it; Late Dorset groups returned to the northwest only around 700–800 (sources differ). Meanwhile Dorset people continued to hunt in the Canadian Arctic. Evidence is purely archaeological and dates rest on radiocarbon.

events.t: No dated human occupation in Greenland; Late Dorset Palaeo-Inuit live in the Canadian Arctic and reach northwest Greenland c. 700–800.

sources.title: Geographic Distribution of the Dorset Culture

Austria.polity: Bavarians under Frankish influence; Alemanni in the west; Slavs under Avar rule in the east
Austria.summary: After the Lombards left for Italy in 568, the Bavarians, under Frankish political influence, struggled with Slavs invading from the east, while Alemanni settled in today's Vorarlberg. The Slavs had Avar rulers and at their greatest extent reached Lower Austria, Styria and Carinthia. At Bregenz, a former Roman fort where Christianity survived mixed with pagan cults, the Irish monk Columbanus and his companions worked in 610–612.

events.t: Columbanus and his companions work at Bregenz on Lake Constance (610–612) before he moves on to Italy.
Western Slavs rise against the Avars under Samo (623 or 624); eastern Austria is among the proposed centres of his realm.

Estonia.summary: The ancestors of the Estonians, a Finnic (Finno-Ugric) people rather than Balts, lived in farming communities during the Middle Iron Age (c. 450–800). Small hillforts appear in the pre-Viking period (c. 600–800), probably housing only a few families and serving as centres of local trade and craft. Weapon hoards, often votive, were deposited at the edges of wetlands. Knowledge comes almost entirely from archaeology.

events.t: Small hillforts, centres of local trade and handicraft, begin to appear in the pre-Viking period (c. 600–800).

sources.title: Martti Veldi, A landscape biography of the 'Land of Drumlins': Vooremaa, East Estonia (PhD thesis, 2020), ch. 8

Latvia.summary: Baltic-speaking peoples, ancestors of the Latvians, lived in the region. Cut off by sea, forest and swamp, the western Balts kept their own identity and pagan religion until the Middle Ages. No written records survive from this period: the documented history of the Latvians begins only in the 13th century, so knowledge comes from archaeology.

events.t: Pagan Baltic communities live without writing; Latvian recorded history begins only in the 13th century.

Lithuania.summary: Baltic-speaking ancestors of the Lithuanians kept their pagan religion until the Middle Ages; their written history begins only in the 13th century. Archaeology shows a long tradition of horse burial: in western and central Lithuania people were buried with whole horses or with horse heads and legs. Migration-period (4th–6th century) graves contain many weapons and non-local goods.

events.t: Burials with whole horses, or horse heads and legs, continue in western and central Lithuania.

sources.title: Piličiauskienė et al., "Horses in Lithuania in the Late Roman–Medieval Period (3rd–14th C AD) Burial Sites", Animals (2022)
